subject: science
passage: In one species of butterfly common in the temperate woodlands of Europe and Asia, adults that emerge in early spring have dark wings, while those that emerge in midsummer are much paler. Because both forms belong to a single species, the difference is thought to be triggered by conditions during development. Entomologist Chidi Okonkwo argues that the trigger is temperature, with cool conditions during the caterpillar stage producing dark adults. Others favor daylength, noting that the caterpillars of the spring generation grow up during the shortening days of autumn, which are also cool.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Okonkwo's argument?

choices.A: Caterpillars kept warm under short days became pale adults, while those kept cold under long days became dark.
choices.B: Dark-winged adults warmed up faster in cool early-morning sunlight than did the pale-winged adults of the same species.
choices.C: Adults emerging in early spring had darker wings than adults of the same species that emerged in midsummer.
choices.D: Caterpillars reared at one steady temperature became dark or pale adults depending only on the daylength they experienced.

explanation.why: In nature, cool temperatures and short days come together in autumn, so either could be the trigger. An experiment that pairs short days with warmth and long days with cold separates them. If wing color follows temperature in both pairings, temperature is the trigger, as Okonkwo argues.
explanation.A: Correct. Wing color tracks temperature even when daylength points the other way, which isolates temperature as the trigger.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This describes an advantage of dark wings in cool weather, not what triggers their development.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This only restates the seasonal difference that both explanations are trying to account for.
explanation.D: Incorrect. Color that depends only on daylength, with temperature held steady, supports the rival explanation and weakens Okonkwo.
